Data Sets

https://github.com/the-pudding/data/tree/master/clinics

Clinics Data

  • Data Source: https://github.com/the-pudding/data/tree/master/clinics
    The source of the data is Github, collected by Russel Goldenberg. The source is reliable as The Pudding is known for providing data and insights, as well as it’s purpose primarily serving a project looking at the distance for cities to abortion clinics.

  • Data Meaning: What does the data represent? How is the information it contains relevant to the content of your first data set?
    The data represents

  • Data Join:
    We intend to join the ‘state’, ‘city’, ‘population’, using the state and city as the common feature. We will need to either total all the data by state across all years or organize all data by years and then by state. We will also mutate the columns across both data sets as Clinics uses full state and city names while Pregnancy uses abbreviated state names.

  • Data Observations: Describe the column names, the number of rows, and some example data (e.g., using glimpse()). 

  • Data Issues: Are there any missings, implausible values, or other data quality issues in the relevant variables? How many? Does this impact the reliability of the data source?

Pregnancy Data

  • Data Source: https://osf.io/kthnf/overview
    The source is Open Science Framework where the data was collected by Isaac Maddow-Zimet, Kathryn Kost, Sean Finn, and Doris W. Chiu. The source is reliable as the data was produced by the Guttmacher Institute which is known for it’s work focusing on sexual and reproductive health rights globally. It was also produced for research analyzing reproductive health patterns and is sourced on a well-known academic platform.

  • Data Meaning: What does the data represent? How is the information it contains relevant to the content of your first data set? The data represents the rates of pregnancy, births, abortions, and miscarriages from different states across several years. This information is relevant as it provides more numerical insights into pregnancy and abortion statistically rather than focusing on the physical locations of abortion clinics relative to different cities.

  • Data Join:
    We intend to join the ‘state’, ‘year’, ‘population1544’, ‘abortionstotal’, ‘birthstotal’, ‘pregnancyratetotal’ ‘birthratetotal’, and ‘abortionratetotal’ using the state and city as the common feature. We will need to either total all the data by state across all years or organize all data by years and then by state. We will also mutate the columns across both data sets as Clinics uses full state and city names while Pregnancy uses abbreviated state names.

  • Data Observations: Describe the column names, the number of rows, and some example data (e.g., using glimpse()). 

  • Data Issues: The data is almost completely full, where there are almost zero missing values and all statistics have been recorded and organized by state, year, and

Join Data

library(dplyr)
  
pregnancy_df <- pregnancy_df |> 
  filter(year == 2017) |>
  select(state, abortionstotal, birthstotal, pregnancyratetotal, birthratetotal, abortionratetotal)

clinics_df <- clinics_df |>
  select(city, state, population, gestation_8_duration, gestation_12_duration, gestation_16_duration, gestation_20_duration)

states <- data.frame(
    state_abb = c(state.abb, "DC"), state_name = c(state.name, "District of Columbia")
  )

clinics_df <- clinics_df |>
  left_join(states, by = c("state" = "state_name"))

completedata <- left_join(clinics_df, pregnancy_df, by = c("state_abb" = "state")) |>
  arrange(state)

Codebook:

https://guttinst.github.io/National-State-Pregnancy-Codebook-1973-2020/

Relevant Variables:

city, state, and state_abb were the keys for the join and identifies location. Population is the variable for the city’s population from the clinics data, and it shows us how many people live in the places we measure. gestation_8_duration to gestation_20_duration measure how long it takes to get to a clinic that provides abortion care at different timings in pregnancy. Variables gestation_8_duration to gestation_20_duration are the most useful variables for our question because they are the core to our access measure.

Potential Biases:

Our combined data is missing some context. The clinics data is by city and the pregnancy data is only by state. Every city in a state therefore gets the same state level rate, and that would not show us the differences between urban and rural areas. The data is also limited to 2017, which is the only year the clinics data covers, so we can’t see the effects of laws passed later than 2017. In addition, none of the datasets includes income, insurance, or ethnicity, so it’s hard to see who can actually reach a clinic because of these inequities. On privacy, the data is combined and has no individuals. On fairness and non discrimination, since we’re missing demographics make, it’s hard to see who is disadvantaged. On transparency, both sources are documented and available for the public to see. We have no way to make sure responsibility beyond documenting our choices, and we should be careful to prevent exaggerating our claims.

Combined Data Wrangling

Cleaning Rows:

clean_data <- completedata |>
  filter(!is.na(state_abb),
         !is.na(gestation_12_duration),
         !is.na(abortionratetotal))
nrow(completedata)
[1] 749
nrow(clean_data)
[1] 749

We removed rows that were missing the values we need or that couldn’t be matched to a state. This way it will keeps the graph and summary from being messed up by incomplete rows.

New Numeric Column:

clean_data <- clean_data |>
  mutate(duration_increase = gestation_20_duration - gestation_8_duration)

We made duration_increase which is the difference between 20 week and 8 week, and this shows how much harder it gets to reach care later in pregnancy.

New Categorical Column:

median_12 <- median(clean_data$gestation_12_duration, na.rm = TRUE)
clean_data <- clean_data |>
  mutate(travel_category = if_else(gestation_12_duration > median_12,
                                   "longer travel", "shorter travel"))
clean_data |> count(travel_category)
  travel_category   n
1   longer travel 180
2  shorter travel 569

We made travel_category to split cities into shorter travel and longer travel relative to the median 12 week duration, and this makes it easier to compare groups of cities.

CODING NOTES

We had to use the state dataset in our join due to the difference in how the states were named. In the Clinics data, the states were named by their full name while the Pregnancy data listed states by the abbreviations. I found the tool through troubleshooting with ChatGPT and Claude and also the following link: https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/datasets/versions/3.3/topics/state
